scope: Curated within Regeneration Atlas only. Not an exhaustive literature review; OPEN_IN_ATLAS is not a claim that science has never addressed this question.

stages.title: Gene / identity
stages.description: Gene or target identity and relevant relationships

stages.title: Human outcome
stages.description: Clinical study and its outcome, including negative results

gaps.title: Does the PROX1 transfer brake operate therapeutically in human retina?
gaps.question: Does blocking extracellular PROX1 transfer produce durable, safely integrated replacement retinal neurons in living human eyes?
gaps.whyOpen: Mouse intervention results, human donor-tissue localization, and human clinical outcomes represent different levels of evidence.
gaps.caveat: Do not treat human PROX1 localization as proof of repair or globally suppress an essential identity regulator.
gaps.studyDesign: Seek independent confirmation in relevant human models, evidence of mature circuit integration, longitudinal functional outcomes, and targeted safety evaluations.

checkpoints.explanation: PROX1 orthology and a human donor retinal observation are curated.
Extracellular PROX1 transfer was investigated as an inhibitory mechanism in mouse retina.
Mouse experiments report neuronal regeneration and delayed vision decline, with durability limitations.
No demonstrated living-human therapy restoring functional retinal neurons is curated.

gaps.title: Which ASCL1 retinal injury program carries across species?
gaps.question: Why does zebrafish ascl1a support injury-induced regeneration, while adult mouse Ascl1 reprogramming needs added interventions?
gaps.whyOpen: Fish paralog identity, injury-stage signaling, and adult mammalian chromatin accessibility may each affect what experiments establish.
gaps.caveat: The zebrafish ascl1a result cannot be assigned to ascl1b; a fish result is not a human intervention.
gaps.studyDesign: Compare cell-state observations and functional outcomes in matched injury contexts; validate paralog-specific roles rather than assuming equivalence.

checkpoints.explanation: Zebrafish ascl1a/ascl1b and mouse/human ASCL1 relationships are explicitly curated.
Fish ascl1a perturbation and experimental adult mouse Ascl1 reprogramming are separately documented.
Adult zebrafish regenerate retinal neurons; mouse intervention produces some neuron-like functional responses.
A proven ASCL1-based restorative retinal therapy in living humans is not curated.

gaps.title: Does optic-nerve axon growth yield correctly connected human circuits?
gaps.question: What evidence distinguishes axon outgrowth from stable, target-appropriate synapses and meaningful visual recovery?
gaps.whyOpen: The cited mouse dual-deletion result measures sustained axon regrowth; the human clinical step is a different claim.
gaps.caveat: PTEN is a tumor suppressor. This question does not endorse PTEN deletion or any unsupervised gene manipulation.
gaps.studyDesign: Track independent anatomical, electrophysiological, behavioral, and safety endpoints in clearly identified experimental models.

checkpoints.explanation: Mammalian PTEN orthology and zebrafish Pten co-orthologs are curated; SOCS3 is in the source-linked pathway map.
Mouse pathway work reports separate PTEN/mTOR and SOCS3/STAT signaling constraints.
Sustained mouse axon regrowth is reported, but full circuit restoration is not established by that record.
No safe and effective human PTEN/SOCS3 optic-nerve regeneration therapy is profiled.

gaps.title: Can adult human retinal preprint signals survive replication and integration tests?
gaps.question: Are the reported adult-donor retinal neural-lineage markers reproducible and associated with truly functional neuronal integration?
gaps.whyOpen: A 2026 donor-tissue study is a preprint, which is an important distinction from peer-reviewed and in-vivo results.
gaps.caveat: Proliferation or neuronal markers alone cannot establish restored vision; treat the preprint as provisional.
gaps.studyDesign: Compare independent donor tissue studies, cell identities, electrophysiology, synaptic connectivity, and eventual peer-reviewed validation.

checkpoints.explanation: FGF2 and GSK3 signaling interventions are named in a donor-tissue preprint; this atlas has no complete orthology panel for them.
Preprint reports cultured human Müller glia responses under these experimental conditions.
A functional retinal circuit replacement outcome is not demonstrated in the cited human donor cultures.
No living-human visual treatment result follows from an ex-vivo preprint.

gaps.title: Is PRRX1 involved in analogous repair roles across zebrafish hearts and axolotl limbs?
gaps.question: Which PRRX1 functions, if any, are shared across heart injury and limb-blastema biology?
gaps.whyOpen: Zebrafish prrx1b loss-of-function affects heart regeneration; axolotl Prrx1 blastema studies include expression and lineage observations.
gaps.caveat: Different tissues and experimental methods do not demonstrate an interchangeable or universal regeneration switch.
gaps.studyDesign: Compare lineage-specific roles using compatible outcome definitions; require perturbation evidence before claiming an axolotl gene is necessary.

checkpoints.explanation: PRRX1 orthology, zebrafish duplicated genes, and axolotl Prrx1 nomenclature are curated.
A fish heart perturbation exists, while axolotl blastema evidence here is observational rather than causal.
Adult zebrafish heart regeneration and axolotl limb regrowth are independently reported at different tissue scales.
Cultured human fetal cells do not establish regeneration of an injured adult human heart or limb.

gaps.title: What closes the neonatal mouse heart repair window?
gaps.question: Which age-dependent constraints distinguish reported neonatal mouse cardiac repair from limited adult human heart-cell turnover?
gaps.whyOpen: Neonatal mouse repair and adult human cardiomyocyte renewal are different observations, not different amounts of a single proven therapy.
gaps.caveat: The neonatal mouse result varies with model and injury details, and should not be generalized to adult mice or humans.
gaps.studyDesign: Separate age, injury method, proliferation, scar architecture, and restored cardiac function in cross-stage comparisons.

checkpoints.explanation: No causal gene-level developmental driver is assigned to this comparison by the current atlas.
The neonatal mouse period and adult human turnover have been studied with distinct methods.
Neonatal mouse repair was reported under specific conditions; adult humans show low-level renewal rather than full regrowth.
Rebuilding a large adult human myocardial injury is not established by either cited result.

gaps.title: When does skin YAP–EN1 signaling drive scarring versus repair?
gaps.question: Under which cell-specific contexts does interfering with the YAP–EN1 scarring program produce stable normal tissue repair?
gaps.whyOpen: Mouse skin fibroblast experiments show promising structural outcomes, while YAP signaling performs different roles elsewhere.
gaps.caveat: A skin fibroblast-specific mouse result does not justify systemic YAP inhibition or claim a scar-free human treatment.
gaps.studyDesign: Seek independent replication, cell-subtype specificity, durability, appendage function, and safety evidence in appropriate models.

checkpoints.explanation: Mouse and human YAP1-related orthology is curated.
A published mouse study links mechanotransduction to EN1-associated fibroblast scarring.
Wounds displayed regenerative features in mice; no general human endpoint is inferred.
The current atlas has no proven human scar-free YAP-targeting therapy.

gaps.title: What can we learn from anti-Nogo-A's nonsignificant clinical primary outcome?
gaps.question: Which endpoints and injury subgroups can be studied prospectively without treating exploratory signals as confirmed benefits?
gaps.whyOpen: The phase 2b primary endpoint was not met in the overall population; that is a result, not a missing experiment.
gaps.caveat: Do not reframe a negative overall trial as success on the strength of subgroup exploration.
gaps.studyDesign: Separate prespecified clinical endpoints, exploratory subgroup findings, patient heterogeneity, and anatomical measures in future research reviews.

checkpoints.explanation: The clinical antibody targets Nogo-A/RTN4, but this release has no R3 orthology panel for it.
Nogo-A is a growth-inhibitory target, but a clinical mechanism is not established by an overall negative endpoint.
The randomized trial reported no statistically significant overall primary motor-function benefit.
A human trial exists; its overall primary endpoint was not met. Documented does NOT mean successful.

gaps.title: How do injury location and age govern mammalian fingertip regrowth?
gaps.question: Which tissue boundaries separate distal digit repair from full limb regeneration in mammals?
gaps.whyOpen: Adult mouse distal digit studies and selected childhood human fingertip case reports are not equivalent to whole-limb regrowth.
gaps.caveat: Do not infer wound treatment instructions or predictable clinical outcomes from a small historical human case series.
gaps.studyDesign: Compare injury anatomy, age, nail-associated tissues, skeletal restoration, and long-term function in independently documented cases.

checkpoints.explanation: Mouse distal digit evidence includes nail-associated Wnt signaling, not a complete conserved pathway map.
Distal mouse nail-region signaling is implicated; the human case series does not establish the same pathway.
Mouse digit-tip anatomical regrowth and selected pediatric fingertip outcomes are reported in different settings.
A small human case series exists; full human limb regeneration is not established.

gaps.title: Does myostatin-associated hypertrophy improve actual repair?
gaps.question: How can increased muscle mass be distinguished from stronger function and regeneration of injured human muscle?
gaps.whyOpen: Human loss-of-function genetics establishes a muscle growth effect, not a regenerative treatment benefit.
gaps.caveat: The genetics must not be misrepresented as an intervention, nor muscle size as repaired muscle quality.
gaps.studyDesign: Review separately quantified strength, motor function, repair after injury, and adverse outcomes; distinguish genetic cases from trials.

checkpoints.explanation: A human MSTN loss-of-function variant is documented in the foundational ledger.
The R1 network records myostatin as a muscle-growth restraint.
Pronounced muscle size was observed, but improved post-injury repair was not demonstrated by that report.
No proven muscle-regeneration treatment is established in the selected human genetics evidence.
